lessons.title: Interfaces, addresses, routes and ARP
lessons.goal:
Learn the four things every network connection needs: an interface, an address, a route and (on Ethernet) a neighbour entry, and read each with the `ip` command.

Why it matters: "the network is down" breaks into these questions. `ip addr`, `ip route` and `ip neigh` answer them in seconds.

setup.note: These steps build three network namespaces joined by virtual cables (veth pairs): lab-a (10.200.1.1) <-> lab-b, the router (10.200.1.2 and 10.200.2.1) <-> lab-c (10.200.2.2). They use sudo, do not touch your real network, and are removed at the end.
commands: for n in lab-a lab-b lab-c; do sudo ip netns del $n 2>/dev/null; done; true
for n in lab-a lab-b lab-c; do sudo ip netns add $n; sudo ip -n $n link set lo up; done
sudo ip link add va type veth peer name vb1; sudo ip link set va netns lab-a; sudo ip link set vb1 netns lab-b
sudo ip link add vb2 type veth peer name vc; sudo ip link set vb2 netns lab-b; sudo ip link set vc netns lab-c
sudo ip -n lab-a addr add 10.200.1.1/24 dev va; sudo ip -n lab-b addr add 10.200.1.2/24 dev vb1; sudo ip -n lab-b addr add 10.200.2.1/24 dev vb2; sudo ip -n lab-c addr add 10.200.2.2/24 dev vc
sudo ip -n lab-a link set va up; sudo ip -n lab-b link set vb1 up; sudo ip -n lab-b link set vb2 up; sudo ip -n lab-c link set vc up
sudo ip netns exec lab-b sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
sudo ip -n lab-a route add 10.200.2.0/24 via 10.200.1.2; sudo ip -n lab-c route add 10.200.1.0/24 via 10.200.2.1

steps.title: The loopback interface
steps.text: Every machine has `lo`, a virtual interface for talking to itself. Its address is `127.0.0.1` (IPv4) and `::1` (IPv6). `ip -br` prints a compact table: name, state, addresses.

run.cmd: ip -br link show lo | awk '{print $1, $2, $3}'
ip -br addr show lo

steps.title: A lab network
steps.text:
To show real routing without touching your real network we use three **network namespaces**: each is a private copy of the network stack (own interfaces, addresses, routes). They are connected by virtual cables (`veth` pairs). `lab-b` is a router between `lab-a` and `lab-c`.

`lab-a` 10.200.1.1 --- 10.200.1.2 `lab-b` 10.200.2.1 --- 10.200.2.2 `lab-c`

run.cmd: ip netns list | awk '{print $1}' | sort | tr '\n' ' '; echo
sudo ip -n lab-b -4 -br addr | sed -E 's/@if[0-9]+//'

steps.title: Addresses
steps.text: `ip addr` shows the addresses on each interface. `10.200.1.1/24` means: this host is 10.200.1.1 on a network of 256 addresses (the `/24` is the **prefix length**; the netmask is 255.255.255.0).

run.cmd: sudo ip -n lab-a -4 -br addr | sed -E 's/@if[0-9]+//'
sudo ip -n lab-a -4 -o addr show dev va | awk '{print $4, $5, $6}'

steps.title: Routes
steps.text: The **routing table** tells the kernel where to send a packet for each destination. The **connected** route (`proto kernel scope link`) was added automatically when the address was assigned. We added a second route by hand: to reach 10.200.2.0/24 go **via** the router 10.200.1.2. `ip route get` shows the decision for one destination.

run.cmd: sudo ip -n lab-a route
run.output:
10.200.1.0/24 dev va proto kernel scope link src 10.200.1.1 
10.200.2.0/24 via 10.200.1.2 dev va

run.cmd: sudo ip -n lab-a route get 10.200.2.2 | sed -E 's/ uid .*//'

steps.under: For each outgoing packet the kernel does a **longest-prefix match** in the routing table and picks the most specific route. `default via X` (0.0.0.0/0) matches anything not matched by a longer prefix. The route also fixes the outgoing interface and the source address.

steps.title: Reach across the router
steps.text: `ping` sends ICMP echo requests. The packets cross `lab-b` because forwarding is on. `traceroute -n` shows each hop by sending packets with increasing TTL.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-a ping -c 2 -W 1 10.200.2.2 | grep -E 'transmitted|rtt' | sed -E 's/, time [0-9]+ms//; s/rtt.*= /rtt min\/avg\/max\/mdev = /; s/[0-9.]+\/[0-9.]+\/[0-9.]+\/[0-9.]+ ms/(numbers vary)/'
run.output:
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = (numbers vary)

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-a traceroute -n -q1 -w1 10.200.2.2 | awk 'NR>1 {print $1, $2}'

steps.title: ARP: from IP address to MAC address
steps.text: On Ethernet a packet goes to a **MAC address**. The **neighbour table** (ARP for IPv4) maps the next hop's IP to its MAC. The kernel asks `who has 10.200.1.2?` and remembers the answer for a while. The next hop of `lab-a` is the router, even for traffic to `lab-c`.

run.cmd: sudo ip -n lab-a neigh | sed -E 's/lladdr [0-9a-f:]+/lladdr <mac>/'

steps.title: Forwarding makes a router
steps.text: A Linux host forwards packets between interfaces only when `net.ipv4.ip_forward` is 1. Switch it off in `lab-b` and the ping fails; switch it on again and it works.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-b sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=0
sudo ip netns exec lab-a ping -c 1 -W 1 10.200.2.2 | grep -E 'transmitted' | sed -E 's/, time [0-9]+ms//'
sudo ip netns exec lab-b sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1; sudo ip netns exec lab-a ping -c 1 -W 1 10.200.2.2 | grep -E 'transmitted' | sed -E 's/, time [0-9]+ms//'
run.output:
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
1 packets transmitted, 1 received, 0% packet loss

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: Deleting a namespace removes its interfaces.

run.cmd: for n in lab-a lab-b lab-c; do sudo ip netns del $n; done; ip netns list | wc -l | awk '{print $1, "namespaces left"}'

options: Address 10.200.1.1 on a network with a 24-bit prefix (256 addresses)

quiz.q: Which command shows which route and source address the kernel picks for a destination?
What happens when `net.ipv4.ip_forward` is 0 on a router?
options: It does not forward packets between interfaces
quiz.explain: Forwarding is off by default; hosts are not routers.

quiz.q: What does the neighbour (ARP) table map?
options: Next-hop IP addresses to MAC addresses

check.scenario: From a server you can ping a host on your own subnet but not one in another subnet. What do you check on the server, in order?
check.answer: `ip addr` (correct address and prefix), `ip route` (is there a route or default gateway for the other subnet? `ip route get DEST`), `ip neigh` (can it resolve the gateway's MAC), then ping the gateway itself, then the far side. If the gateway answers but the far host does not, the problem is on the router (forwarding, its routes or a firewall).

lessons.title: NetworkManager and persistent network configuration
lessons.goal:
Learn why `ip addr add` is temporary, and how NetworkManager stores connections that survive a reboot, using `nmcli` on a harmless dummy interface.

Why it matters: on Red Hat family systems (and many desktops) NetworkManager owns the network configuration. Changes made with `ip` are lost at reboot or overwritten when NM reconfigures an interface.

setup.note: Steps here create and delete a dummy network connection with NetworkManager.
commands: sudo nmcli connection delete lab0 2>/dev/null; true

steps.title: Runtime versus persistent
steps.text: The `ip` command changes the **running kernel**. Nothing is written to disk. A **network manager** (NetworkManager, systemd-networkd, netplan, ifupdown) stores configuration in files and applies it at boot and when links change.

run.cmd: systemctl is-active NetworkManager
nmcli -f DEVICE,TYPE,STATE device status | head -n 2
run.output:
DEVICE           TYPE      STATE                  
enp0s6           ethernet  connected

steps.title: Devices and connections
steps.text: NM distinguishes **devices** (the interfaces) from **connections** (saved profiles). A connection is applied to a device. `nmcli connection show` lists profiles.

run.cmd: nmcli -t -f TYPE connection show | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3

steps.title: Create a connection on a dummy interface
steps.text: A **dummy** interface is a virtual interface that goes nowhere: safe for tests. This command creates the profile, the interface and applies a fixed address.

run.cmd: sudo nmcli connection add type dummy ifname lab0 con-name lab0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 10.200.9.1/24 2>&1 | sed -E 's/ \([^)]*\)//'
sleep 1; ip -4 -br addr show lab0

steps.title: Modify and re-apply
steps.text: `nmcli connection modify` changes the stored profile. `connection up` applies it to the device again. The `+` prefix adds a value instead of replacing.

run.cmd: sudo nmcli connection modify lab0 +ipv4.addresses 10.200.9.2/24 && sudo nmcli connection up lab0 > /dev/null; ip -4 -br addr show lab0
nmcli -g ipv4.addresses connection show lab0

steps.title: It is stored in a file
steps.text: NM writes each profile to `/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/NAME.nmconnection` in an INI-like format. That is what survives a reboot.

run.cmd: sudo grep -vE '^(uuid|$)' /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/lab0.nmconnection
run.output:
[connection]
id=lab0
type=dummy
interface-name=lab0
timestamp=1794138062
[dummy]
[ipv4]
address1=10.200.9.1/24
address2=10.200.9.2/24
method=manual
[ipv6]
addr-gen-mode=default
method=disabled
[proxy]

steps.under: NetworkManager talks to the kernel with **netlink** sockets (the same interface `ip` uses), watches link and address events, and reapplies its profiles. If you change an address with `ip` NM may leave it alone, but it can also remove it the next time it re-activates the connection. Always change the profile.

steps.title: Remove it
steps.text: Deleting the profile removes the file and the dummy interface.

run.cmd: sudo nmcli connection delete lab0 2>&1 | sed -E 's/ \([^)]*\)//'
ip -br link show lab0 2>&1 | sed 's/.*: //'

quiz.q: Why is an address added with `ip addr add` lost after a reboot?
options: It is stored in RAM only

quiz.q: What is the difference between a NetworkManager device and a connection?
options: A device is an interface; a connection is a saved profile applied to a device

quiz.q: Which command re-applies a modified profile?

check.scenario: After a reboot a static IP you set with `ip addr add` is gone. Show the right way to set it so it persists, with NetworkManager.
check.answer: `nmcli connection modify "System eth0" ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.0.2.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.0.2.1 ipv4.dns 192.0.2.53` then `nmcli connection up "System eth0"`. Verify with `nmcli -f ipv4 connection show "System eth0"` and `ip -br addr`.

interview.q: What does an IP address with /24 mean?
interview.a: A network prefix of 24 bits: the first 24 bits identify the network, the last 8 the host (256 addresses, 254 usable). See [the lesson](#/lesson/28/interfaces-addresses-routes).

interview.q: How does Linux choose a route?
interview.a: Longest-prefix match in the routing table; `default` is the fallback. `ip route get DEST` shows the choice. See [the lesson](#/lesson/28/interfaces-addresses-routes).
The protocol that resolves a next-hop IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local link; results live in the neighbour table (`ip neigh`).

interview.q: What makes a Linux host a router?
interview.a: `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` (and routes, plus firewall rules that allow forwarding).

interview.q: Why are `ip` changes not permanent and how do you make them so?
interview.a: `ip` changes the running kernel. Persist with the network manager: `nmcli connection modify` (NetworkManager), netplan, or systemd-networkd files. See [NetworkManager](#/lesson/28/networkmanager).
A separate copy of the network stack (interfaces, addresses, routes, firewall rules, sockets). Containers use them; `ip netns` manages them.

glossary.def: A network attachment point of the kernel, such as eth0, lo or a veth.
The number of leading bits that identify the network in an address (/24).
The kernel's list of destinations and where to send packets for them.
The router used for destinations not matched by a more specific route.
Address Resolution Protocol: maps IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses on a link.
A virtual Ethernet cable: two interfaces connected back to back, often in different namespaces.
The service that manages network connections and persistent profiles.
An isolated copy of the network stack.

commands.desc: Show addresses in a compact table.
Show which route will be used for DEST.

commands.cmd: sudo ip addr add 10.0.0.5/24 dev eth0
nmcli connection modify NAME ipv4.addresses A/24
